title: Security basics in designs
summary: Security in a design means naming what an attacker could do at each trust boundary and placing a control there on purpose. This lesson gives threat modelling in one page with the STRIDE table, the OWASP lists of the risks that recur, OAuth 2.0 roles and OpenID Connect with the token validation rules, what the security best-current-practice RFCs require of tokens, authorization and least privilege with the zero trust tenets, tenant isolation in silo and pool models, data, secrets and the audit log, and a worked threat model for one multi-tenant API.

blocks.text: The IETF OAuth working group's 2025 best current practice records decisions that practitioners had reached over a decade: public clients must use PKCE, the implicit grant should not be used, the resource owner password credentials grant must not be used, and refresh tokens for public clients must be sender-constrained or rotated. A design that still relies on any of the retired patterns is out of step with the standard its identity provider implements.

The OWASP API Security project puts broken object level authorization first in both its 2019 and 2023 editions, on the reasoning that APIs expose endpoints handling object identifiers and so create a wide attack surface of object level access control issues, and it instructs that the check be considered in every function that accesses a data source with an id from the user.

subtopics.title: Threat modelling a design in one page

blocks.text: The OWASP threat modelling process starts from a picture of what is being built: a data flow diagram showing external actors, processes, data stores and the flows between them, with the privilege or trust boundaries marked. Entry points are the interfaces through which an attacker can interact with the system or supply it with data, and entry and exit points define a trust boundary. Assets are what you want to protect or what attackers want, with the caveat on the page that assets are often hard to name in advance and can distract. Threats are then enumerated per element with a categorisation, and STRIDE is the one most often used for design-time work.

blocks.caption: The STRIDE threat list and the control each category maps to, from the OWASP process page.
rows: uses another user's credentials, such as a username and password
changes persistent data, or data in transit over an open network
performs a prohibited operation in a system that cannot trace it
reads a file or data in transit without being granted access
makes the service unavailable or unusable to valid users
gains privileged access to information or to compromise the system

blocks.text: The page's mitigation table says what each category is answered with: appropriate authentication and never storing secrets for spoofing; authorization, hashes, message authentication codes and signatures for tampering; signatures, timestamps and audit trails for repudiation; authorization, encryption and protected secrets for disclosure; authentication, authorization, filtering, throttling and quality of service for denial of service; and running with least privilege for elevation. Threats are then classified as unmitigated, partially mitigated or fully mitigated, which is the ranked list a design review reads.

The page also places the exercise in time: threat modelling is not code review, but done early it means the application is built with the mitigations from the start, and it tells reviewers where the entry points are so that review goes depth-first into the risky components rather than breadth-first over everything.

One page: the diagram with its trust boundaries, the entry points, the STRIDE threats per boundary, and a decision per threat to mitigate, accept, transfer or remove the feature. Revisit it when a boundary is added, such as a new public endpoint or a third-party integration.

subtopics.title: The risks that recur: the OWASP lists

blocks.text: Two OWASP lists tell a designer which weaknesses are found most often in real applications, and the 2025 edition's introduction gives the shares of tested applications affected. Broken access control stays first, with server-side request forgery folded into it; security misconfiguration rose to second as more behaviour moves into configuration; software supply chain failures is new as a broad category and had the highest average exploit and impact scores despite few occurrences in the data; and a new tenth category covers mishandling of exceptional conditions, including failing open.

blocks.text: For services the API Security list is the sharper tool, and its first entry is the one that scales with the product. Broken object level authorization arises because APIs expose endpoints that handle object identifiers, so the list's instruction is that object level authorization checks should be considered in every function that accesses a data source using an id from the user. The list also names unrestricted resource consumption, where requests cost bandwidth, CPU, memory, storage or paid third-party calls, and broken function level authorization, where an ordinary user reaches an administrative function.

items: API1 broken object level authorization; API2 broken authentication; API3 broken object property level authorization.
API4 unrestricted resource consumption; API5 broken function level authorization; API6 unrestricted access to sensitive business flows.
API7 server side request forgery; API8 security misconfiguration; API9 improper inventory management; API10 unsafe consumption of APIs.

blocks.text: The top risk is not an exotic exploit but a handler that trusts an id in the request. Every function that takes an object id checks that the caller may act on that object; a role check alone is not enough.

subtopics.title: Authentication: OAuth 2.0 roles and OpenID Connect

blocks.text: OAuth 2.0 defines four roles, and most confusion about tokens comes from not naming them. The resource owner grants access, and is called the end-user when a person. The resource server hosts the protected resources and accepts requests bearing access tokens. The client makes requests on the resource owner's behalf, wherever it runs. The authorization server issues access tokens after authenticating the resource owner and obtaining authorization, and one authorization server may issue tokens accepted by many resource servers. In the authorization code grant the client receives a code via the user's browser and exchanges it for tokens on a back channel; the client credentials grant lets a client obtain a token with only its own credentials, which is the basis of service-to-service identity.

blocks.caption: The four OAuth 2.0 roles, and who plays them in a typical web application.
rows: an entity able to grant access to a protected resource
an application making protected resource requests on the owner's behalf
the web or mobile app, or a calling service
issues access tokens after authenticating the owner and obtaining authorization
hosts protected resources; accepts and responds to requests with access tokens

blocks.text: OpenID Connect is the identity layer on top of OAuth 2.0: it adds an ID token, a JSON Web Token carrying claims about the authentication of the end-user by the authorization server, with an issuer, a subject, an audience and an expiry. The authorization code flow returns the code to the client and the tokens from the token endpoint, so the tokens never pass through the browser.

blocks.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram
  participant U as User browser
  participant A as Application
  participant I as Identity provider
  participant S as API service
  U->>A: Open protected page
  A->>U: Redirect to login with code challenge
  U->>I: Authenticate
  I->>U: Redirect back with authorization code
  U->>A: Deliver code
  A->>I: Exchange code and verifier for tokens
  I->>A: ID token, access token, refresh token
  A->>S: Call API with access token
  S->>S: Verify signature, issuer, audience, expiry, scope
  S->>A: Response
blocks.legend: The authorization code flow with PKCE: the code travels through the browser, the tokens do not; the API validates the access token on every call (s3, s4, s5).

items: The issuer identifier obtained during discovery must exactly match the iss claim.
The aud claim must contain the client's own client_id; a token that does not list the client, or lists untrusted audiences, is rejected.
The signature is validated with the keys the issuer publishes, and the current time must be before the exp claim, allowing small clock skew.
A nonce sent in the request must come back in the token and be checked against replay.

blocks.text: Delegate login to an identity provider with the authorization code flow, and validate every token on every call: issuer, audience, signature, expiry. An application that stores passwords or parses tokens without validating them has already failed the first STRIDE row.

subtopics.title: Tokens: what the best current practices require

blocks.text: The IETF's security best current practice for OAuth 2.0, published in 2025, retires the shortcuts. Public clients must use PKCE, which binds the code exchange to a secret the client generated, to prevent authorization code injection; for confidential clients it is recommended. Clients should not use the implicit grant or any response type that delivers an access token in the authorization response. The resource owner password credentials grant must not be used, because it exposes the user's credentials to the client and trains users to type them in the wrong place. Refresh tokens for public clients must be sender-constrained or rotated, and servers should sender-constrain access tokens with mutual TLS or DPoP so that a stolen token cannot be replayed from elsewhere.

blocks.caption: The token rules of RFC 9700.
rows: prevents injection and misuse of authorization codes
the same protection, and CSRF prevention as a side effect
tokens in the authorization response leak and can be injected
exposes credentials to the client; cannot carry two-factor flows
a stolen or leaked token is useless to another sender
Refresh tokens for public clients sender-constrained or rotated
limits what a stolen refresh token can do

blocks.text: The JWT best current practice governs the receiving side. Libraries must let the caller specify the set of acceptable algorithms and must use no other, the alg header must match the operation performed, and each key is used with exactly one algorithm. When a token carries an issuer, the keys used must belong to that issuer, which OpenID Connect arranges by publishing a JWK set at an https address found through the issuer's metadata; when an issuer serves more than one relying party, the token must carry an audience and the recipient must reject a token whose audience is absent or not its own.

Together the two documents fix the token lifetimes a design should expect: short-lived access tokens validated statelessly at the resource server, with revocation handled by expiry rather than by lookup, and longer-lived refresh tokens held only by the client that can prove it is the client, rotated on use. Service-to-service calls use the client credentials grant or a workload identity with mutual TLS rather than a shared static key, which is also the first design principle of the AWS security pillar: centralise identity and aim to eliminate reliance on long-term static credentials.

An access token validated only for its signature is accepted from any issuer, for any audience, with any algorithm the attacker chose. Pin the algorithms, the issuer and the audience, and reject a missing audience.

subtopics.title: Authorization, least privilege and zero trust

blocks.text: Authentication says who the caller is; authorization decides what the caller may do, and it is enforced on the server for every request. The API Security list's object, function and property level entries are all authorization: object level, where the handler must check that this caller may act on this object; function level, where an administrative operation must not be reachable by an ordinary role; and property level, where a response or an update must not expose or accept fields the caller is not entitled to. Role-based rules decide the function; the object and the property need the ownership or tenant relation, which must come from the verified token and the stored record, never from a client-supplied field.

Least privilege applies the same discipline to machines. The AWS security pillar's first principle is a strong identity foundation: least privilege and separation of duties with appropriate authorization for each interaction, centralised identity management, and the elimination of long-term static credentials. In a design that means one identity per service with only the permissions its call paths need, a read-only database role for a read service, and network policy that allows only the declared paths, so that a compromised component reaches little.

Zero trust, in the words of NIST's architecture document rather than a vendor's, is a set of tenets about access decisions, not a product. The central one is that network location alone does not imply trust: a request from inside the old perimeter meets the same requirements as one from anywhere else, and every communication is secured and source-authenticated.

blocks.caption: The zero trust tenets of NIST SP 800-207, condensed.
columns: what it asks of a design
rows: All data sources and computing services are resources
every service and store is a thing to be authorized to, including small devices and SaaS
All communication is secured regardless of network location
encrypt and authenticate internal calls as if they crossed the internet
Access to individual resources is granted per session
evaluate trust before each access, with least privilege, and do not let one grant imply another
Access is determined by dynamic policy
the decision uses client identity, the application and the requesting asset's state, plus behavioural and environmental attributes
The enterprise monitors and measures the integrity and security posture of all assets
no asset is inherently trusted; posture feeds the decision
Authentication and authorization are strictly enforced before access
a dynamic, continuous cycle of scanning, evaluating and reevaluating
The enterprise collects as much information as possible about assets, infrastructure and communications
and uses it to improve policy

blocks.text: Deny by default. Decide function access by role, object and property access by the relation between the verified caller and the stored record, and give every machine identity the least it needs. Treat the internal network as untrusted.

A multi-tenant design has one more boundary than a single-tenant one: between tenants. AWS's tenant isolation whitepaper names the two ends of the spectrum. In the silo model each tenant runs a fully separate stack of resources surrounded by shared identity, onboarding, metering, deployment and operations; isolation is an end-to-end construct around the whole stack, generally simpler to enforce with well-defined constructs, at a cost to the economies of scale and agility that make SaaS attractive. In the pool model tenants share some or all of the infrastructure, which scales in proportion to actual load, and the storage is shared too, a table indexed by tenant identifier.

blocks.caption: Silo against pool, from the whitepaper.
rows: shared compute and storage, tenants side by side
a boundary around the whole stack; networking and IAM constructs apply
those constructs cannot separate tenants; isolation must be built into the application and the data access
per tenant; trades efficiency for compliance or domain needs
in proportion to actual load; the efficiency SaaS is after
cross-tenant access through a shared path; the whitepaper calls for special diligence

blocks.text: The whitepaper's warning is the design rule: a shared model increases the chance of cross-tenant access and cannot be a reason to relax isolation. In a pooled design that means the tenant identifier is carried from the verified token into every query, enforced in the data layer as well as the handler, so that a handler bug cannot read another tenant's rows; that encryption keys, queues and caches are keyed by tenant where the blast radius justifies it; and that the noisy-neighbour problem, one tenant's load degrading another's, is treated with quotas and fairness controls as an availability threat.

Many products mix the models by tier: pooled resources for the standard tier and siloed stacks for tenants with compliance requirements, with the same identity and onboarding across both. The threat model gains a column for each: which tenant boundary a flow crosses and which control enforces it.

Carry the tenant id from the verified token, never from the request body, apply it in every query, and enforce it in the storage layer as well as the handler. Pooling raises the standard; it does not lower it.

subtopics.title: Protecting data, secrets and the audit trail

blocks.text: The AWS security pillar states the data principles a design should carry by default: classify data into sensitivity levels and protect it in transit and at rest with encryption, tokenisation and access control; keep people away from data by removing the need for direct access and manual handling; maintain traceability by monitoring, alerting and auditing actions and changes in real time; apply security at every layer; automate the controls as code; and prepare for security events with rehearsed incident response.

blocks.caption: The AWS security pillar's design principles and what each means in a design document.
rows: central identity, least privilege, no long-term static credentials
audit events emitted and alerted on; logs integrated with investigation tooling
edge, network, load balancer, host, application and code each have a control
controls defined as code in version-controlled templates
Protect data in transit and at rest
classification, TLS on every hop, encryption at rest with managed keys
no direct production data access; tooling instead
an incident process, simulations, automated detection and recovery

blocks.text: Secrets are data with a short useful life. Database passwords, API keys and signing keys belong in a secrets manager and are injected at runtime, never committed to source control or baked into images; they are rotated so that a stolen credential works only briefly, and where the platform allows, issued dynamically per workload or session so that there is nothing long-lived to steal. The pillar's phrase for the goal is to eliminate reliance on long-term static credentials.

The audit trail is the control for repudiation and the input to detection. The OWASP logging cheat sheet lists what to always log: input and output validation failures, authentication successes and failures, authorization failures, session management failures such as suspicious JWT validation failures, application errors, start-ups and shut-downs, and higher-risk actions such as user administration, use of administrative or break-glass accounts, access to sensitive data, key use and rotation, and data export. It is equally clear about what to exclude: passwords, session identification values and access tokens.

Log security events with enough context to investigate, to a store the application cannot alter, and alert on them; the 2025 Top 10 renamed its logging category to say that logging without alerting is of little value. Never log a secret.

worked_example.title: Worked example: the one-page threat model and controls for a multi-tenant invoicing API

blocks.text: A small invoicing product exposes an API to its tenants' finance teams and to a mobile app. The counts below are assumptions chosen to make the exercise concrete; the controls follow the teaching, and the code after the steps shows the two checks that matter most.

blocks.title: From data flow diagram to controls
items: Diagram: 3 external actors (browser, mobile app, a payment provider's webhook), 2 processes (API, worker), 2 stores (database, object storage) (assumption).
Trust boundaries: 4, between the internet and the edge, the edge and the API, the API and the stores, and between tenants inside the shared database.
Entry points: 14 endpoints and one webhook (assumption), each listed with the trust level it requires.
STRIDE over the boundaries: 6 categories times 4 boundaries gives 24 candidate threats; ranking by likelihood and effect leaves 7 to mitigate now.
Authentication: the identity provider with the authorization code flow and PKCE for both the web and the mobile client; no password grant.
Token lifetimes: access tokens of 10 minutes (assumption) validated statelessly; refresh tokens rotated on every use for the public mobile client.
Validation at the API: an allow-list of one signing algorithm, the issuer from discovery, the audience equal to the API's own identifier, expiry with 30 seconds of skew.
Object level authorization: every one of the 14 endpoints resolves the invoice and compares its tenant to the tenant claim in the token before doing anything else.
Tenant isolation in the pool: a tenant_id column on every table and a row-level security policy bound to the session's tenant, so a handler bug cannot cross tenants.
Resource consumption: a per-tenant rate limit of 600 requests per minute (assumption) and a 5 MB cap on uploads, against the unrestricted-consumption risk.
Webhook: the payment provider's signature verified before parsing, and the event id stored for replay rejection, against spoofing and tampering on that boundary.
Audit: 8 event classes from the logging list, each carrying the tenant and the caller, written to an append-only store with 400 days of retention (assumption) and alerts on authorization failures.
The decider: object level authorization. Every other control is a library or a platform setting; this one is a check in every handler, and it is the one that fails silently as the product grows.

blocks.caption: The threat model as the review should receive it: one row per ranked threat.
rows: a tenant or a bot exhausts the API
signature, issuer, audience, expiry; sender-constrained refresh
an ordinary user reaches an admin function
an invoice id from another tenant is read
object level check plus row-level policy
a worker writes with a shared credential
one identity per service, least privilege, no static keys
audit event with tenant and caller, append-only store

blocks.code:
import time
import jwt                                   # PyJWT
from jwt import PyJWKClient

ISSUER = "https://id.example.test/realms/invoicing"      # from discovery, pinned
AUDIENCE = "invoicing-api"                                  # this API's own identifier
JWKS = PyJWKClient(f"{ISSUER}/protocol/openid-connect/certs")

def verify(token: str) -> dict:
    key = JWKS.get_signing_key_from_jwt(token).key   # the issuer's published key for this token's kid
    return jwt.decode(
        token, key,
        algorithms=["RS256"],          # an allow-list of one; never the token's own alg
        issuer=ISSUER,                 # iss must match exactly
        audience=AUDIENCE,             # aud must name this API; a missing aud is rejected
        leeway=30,                     # seconds of clock skew on exp
        options={"require": ["exp", "iss", "aud", "sub"]},
    )

def get_invoice(token: str, invoice_id: str, db):
    claims = verify(token)
    tenant = claims["tenant_id"]                       # from the verified token, never from the request
    invoice = db.fetch_one("select * from invoices where id = %s", (invoice_id,))
    if invoice is None or invoice["tenant_id"] != tenant:
        raise Forbidden()                              # object level authorization: the same answer for missing and foreign
    return invoice
blocks.caption: The two checks the example rests on: token validation pinned to one algorithm, the issuer and the audience, and the object level check against the tenant claim.
Row-level security bound to the session's tenant: the second line of defence behind the handler's check.
